name: The Dunning–Kruger Effect
statement: The skills you need to do a task well are the same skills you need to know you are doing it badly.
statementAccent: the same skills you need to know you are doing it badly
meaning: People who are weakest at something tend to rate themselves most generously, because the competence that would let them spot their mistakes is exactly the competence they lack.
example: A new analyst finishes her first pivot table and reports that she is 'basically fluent' in the tool. Two years later, having learned what it can actually do, she rates herself lower than she did in week one — the same person, more skill, less confidence.
whyItMatters: Self-assessment is a poor instrument at the low end of any skill, so hiring, promotion, and self-directed learning all need an external check. The honest reading is narrower than the internet's: it is a claim about noisy self-knowledge, not a licence to call people you disagree with stupid.
origin: Justin Kruger and David Dunning published "Unskilled and Unaware of It" in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology in 1999, based on Cornell studies of humour, logic, and grammar. The finding is robust, but its interpretation is actively debated: critics argue the pattern is substantially produced by regression to the mean and the better-than-average effect rather than a specific metacognitive deficit.

sources.text: Kruger, J., & Dunning, D. (1999). "Unskilled and Unaware of It: How Difficulties in Recognizing One's Own Incompetence Lead to Inflated Self-Assessments." Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 77(6), 1121–1134.
